extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: researchers, educators and practitioners across geology, mineralogy, agriculture, biology, medicine and general science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative norms for scientific books, practical handbooks, and empirical studies (field and laboratory) as illustrated by book reviews and letters discussing experimental design and interpretation. Covers expectations for scope, methods, illustrations, evidence, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise mathematical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The treatment in Part 2 is mathematical without unnecessary refinements.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical sections should be rigorous but avoid gratuitous refinements that do not aid understanding or application; prefer clear, economical presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of scattered literature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Apart from the advantage of the presentation in one volume of much valuable work, hitherto scattered in many books and journals...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing dispersed material together in a single volume is a virtue—systematic treatment can elucidate new points and stimulate further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include weighty suggestions for future research
rubrics_metrics.description: “the suggestions given for future research must carry weight. Dr. Salmon considers that the most pressing point for future research... is the question of the degree of imperfection common in practical direction-fixed ends.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/reviews should identify clear, actionable research priorities and justify them; suggested future work should be plausible and influential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate coverage and illustration of recent advances
rubrics_metrics.description: “The reference to the very important recent work on the elucidation of crystal structure by means of X-rays, however, occupies only slightly more than one page, without a single illustration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important recent developments should be covered in sufficient depth and illustrated where appropriate; brief, unillustrated mentions of major advances are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed methodological sections
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is a much longer and really valuable section on the determination of the refractive indices of microscopic crystals by the more recent improved microscopic methods of F. Becke and F. E. Wright.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear, detailed expositions of improved or modern methods so readers can understand and adopt them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern, scientific classification and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are glad to see that the references to classes of lower than full systematic symmetry as ‘hemihedral’ and ‘tetartohedral’ ... is now only a passing one ... The crystal classes are now referred to as possessing each their own definite elements of symmetry, the only truly scientific method of distinguishing them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid antiquated or misleading nomenclature; adopt classification schemes that reflect current scientific understanding and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive topical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: “The scope of the work is extremely wide and all of the following are dealt with: coal, petroleum, natural gas, metalliferous and non-metalliferous minerals of economic importance, and building stones.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks intended as general treatments should cover the main subtopics relevant to the field to be considered truly comprehensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and clear contribution beyond prior works
rubrics_metrics.description: “The text as a whole shows a great resemblance to that of two of the author’s previous works ... the chapter on oil appears to be a précis ... some parts dealing with mineral deposits have largely the same text and diagrams of the corresponding earlier work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide new synthesis, updated material or fresh analysis rather than reprinting substantial parts of earlier works without clear added value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic balance relative to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is evident that the author has written his ‘General Economic Geology’ primarily for an American public since all his examples, where possible, are from America’ localities, with little or no mention of occurrences of equal or greater importance in other parts of the world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of examples should match intended readership, but authors should acknowledge global contexts where relevant and avoid parochial exclusion if the subject is global.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an excellent bibliography for specialised study
rubrics_metrics.description: “The value of the book is greatly enhanced by the addition of an excellent bibliography, which will allow of a more specialised study of particular areas where required.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide thorough references to facilitate deeper, specialised follow-up by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement text with maps, diagrams and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: “the text throughout is plentifully supplemented with maps, diagrams, and half-tone blocks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual aids (maps, diagrams, photographs, blocks) substantially increase the usefulness and accessibility of scientific texts, especially in fields with geographic or structural content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical handbooks should include case descriptions and economic data
rubrics_metrics.description: “...intended as a practical handbook... supplemented their general discussion by detailed descriptions of actual installations. These accounts include the balance-sheets of the operation, which show that in most of the schemes the increased crops have paid for the outlay in a short time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handbooks aimed at practitioners should present real installations, worked examples and economic analyses (e.g., balance-sheets) that demonstrate feasibility and payback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss legal and organisational context for practical projects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Particular interest attaches to the section dealing with drainage laws, and the manner in which the cost and the benefits of a proposed scheme for a district are divided among the farmers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical manuals should explain relevant laws, cost-sharing arrangements and institutional mechanisms affecting implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include practical appendices and guidance on instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: “The concluding chapter is devoted to the care and use of surveying implements, and a useful appendix of laboratory exercises is provided, in which the main principles of drainage are illustrated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices with instrumentation care, laboratory exercises or worked practical tasks are valuable for pedagogy and field application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate student creative work for smoothness, vocabulary, and absence of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The facility of the verse and, generally, its smoothness suggest... many show a poetic feeling... a considerable command of an appropriate vocabulary. The incongruous, the mark of the unpractised versifier, is commendably absent. ... of the various classes of poems, the carols are by far the most successful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing student verse or compositions value fluency (smoothness), appropriate vocabulary, avoidance of incongruity, and form suitability (some forms work better for novices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical research requires controlled clinical experiments and cautious interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: “What is, of course, needed is a whole series of clinical experiments made with the control and precision of the observations... Experiments of this kind are laborious and difficult. Meanwhile the practical sanitarian can get to work with Sunlight and cod-liver oil and abolish the disease before any one has found out what part of the spectrum is effective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses should be tested by carefully controlled clinical experiments; while awaiting mechanistic proof, practical public-health measures may be prudent; avoid dogmatic claims that neglect clinical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design biological field experiments with known-age cohorts and adequate sample sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: “The proofs for this statement are not yet sufficient to establish it as a fact... actual proof could only be obtained in the most fortuitous circumstances. The kind of result required to amount to proof would be one which gave 1000 individuals all males out of 1000 individuals examined... oysters settle at different intervals over a period of several months, a heterogeneous population with regard to age... Since, however, sex-change may occur very rapidly, a difference in age of a few months... the difficulty.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish robust conclusions, use cohorts of known age, large sample sizes, control heterogeneity (age, growth rates), and plan experiments to avoid confounding due to staggered settlement or growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate laboratory observations with natural population data and across conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The definite information obtained from this one oyster is corroborated by sex-conditions in other young oysters... the conditions in 1921, namely the unusually long warm summer, were highly abnormal, and it is not to be expected that one-year-old female oysters will often occur in British waters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret experimental findings in the light of natural variability, abnormal years, and corroboration from multiple populations/species before generalising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject unsuitable geometric-only methods for paleogeographic reconstructions; demand physical plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “I quite agree with Mr. Lake’s remarks... as to the unsuitability of the tracing-paper method of investigating the merits of Wegener’s hypothesis... For the truth of Wegener’s theory to be accepted we must also believe in a great degree of plasticity for the earth’s crust.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruction methods should not rely solely on superficial geometric fit; they must be compatible with geophysical plausibility (crustal behaviour) and should involve cross-disciplinary evidence (astronomy/physics) for forces and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entomological reproductive studies: document mating habits and parthenogenesis systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of points on saw-flies: e.g., females of Athalia lineolata found greatly outnumbered by males; in certain species males are excessively rare; some species produce males only by parthenogenesis; many species are facultatively parthenogenetic; some refuse to pair in captivity; virgin females may lay eggs parthenogenetically while in presence of males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile species-level lists, observe mating behavior in both field and lab, record cases of facultative vs obligate parthenogenesis, conduct experiments to test hypotheses about regulation of sex ratios and reproductive strategies; use grants/support for sustained study.
